They took her to the boat, rowed out into the middle of the lake, and beat her savagely as a warning to other beggars never to let the secret out. Beggar Li cried her innocence to high heaven; the anguish was unbearable to hear.

paragraphs.zh: 船到向鄉官後門，聞溪中叫死聲，甚可憐，遣二家人去牽其船來，問打何人。眾丐指曰：「打李丐婆。」鄉官問：「因何打？」丐婆不敢說，只苦情求救。鄉官令引丐婆異處，再問曰：「你因何被這等苦打？明說來，我便救你。」李丐婆一一敘其前由。向鄉官聞情淒愴，不勝發忿，即鎖住四棍，並引眾丐入見太府，代陳其冤苦。太府亦切恨之，將四棍各打三十，曰：「此罪雖凌遲碎剮未足懲其罪，可鎖於府前，令眾人共毆之，以洩其忿。」眾人知此棍情，都來手毆石打，四棍一時皮破血吐，立刻盡死。後瞽目、拐腳眾丐，各問其鄉貫，家有人者，令其收養；無親屬者，各送入養濟院。人盡感向鄉官之仁，能除此四孽棍。
paragraphs.en: The boat happened to come by the back gate of a retired official named Xiang. Hearing cries of mortal agony from the creek—pitiful beyond words—he sent two servants to haul the boat in and asked who was being beaten. The beggars pointed and said, “They are beating the beggar woman Li.” The official asked why. The woman dared not say; she only begged in her misery to be saved. He had her led apart from the others and asked again: “Why were you beaten so cruelly? Tell me plainly, and I will save you.” The beggar woman Li told the whole story from the beginning. Hearing it, Xiang was grief-stricken and could not contain his fury. He clapped the four crooks in chains on the spot, led the whole band of beggars in to see the prefect, and laid out their wrongs on their behalf. The prefect too burned with hatred. He had each of the four given thirty strokes and declared: “For a crime like this, even death by slow slicing would not be punishment enough. Chain them in front of the prefecture gate and let the crowd beat them, to vent the people’s rage.” Everyone who knew what these crooks had done came to strike them with fists and stones; in moments the four were torn and vomiting blood, and all died on the spot. Afterward, the blind and crippled beggars were each asked their native place. Those with families were sent home to be cared for; those without kin were placed in poorhouses. The people were all grateful for Xiang’s humanity in rooting out these four swindling fiends.

paragraphs.zh: 按：人家子女幼稚，不可令其單行，亦不可帶金銀鐲錢。若偶遇此等棍，悔何可及！其防於未失之先可也。今後官府遇瞎拐群集處時，遣人查其居止，及提問一二瘸瞎緣由，或訪得此等棍，則除一棍勝去一狼虎也，功德高於浮屠矣。
paragraphs.en: Note: People with young children must never let them go about alone, nor let them wear gold or silver bangles. Should a child chance to meet such crooks, regret comes too late. Guard against the loss before it happens. Henceforth, whenever officials come upon a place where blind and crippled beggars gather, they should send men to find out where they lodge and question one or two of them about how they came to be lame or blind. If crooks like these are unearthed, then removing one crook is better than removing a wolf or a tiger—and the merit of it is higher than any pagoda.

stories.title_en: A Eunuch Cooks Men and Eats Their Essence

paragraphs.zh: 朝廷往往聽言利之臣，命太監四出抽分，名為徵商抑末以重農本，實則商稅重而轉賣之處必貴，則買之價增，而買者受其害；商不通而出物之處必賤，則賣之價減，而賣者受其害。利雖僅取及商，而四民皆陰耗其財，以供朝廷之暗取，尤甚於明加田稅也。且徵榷之利，朝廷得一，太監得十，稅官得百，巡卒得千，是民費千百金，以奉朝廷之一金，益上者少而損下者無涯矣。然巡卒、稅官之實溪壑，猶是普天率土之民得飽暖也。特不耕不織而魚肉下民，不免坐蠹天地間服食。若太監攘剝既多，崇聚盈溢，視錦繡如敝葉，視金玉如瓦礫。服食器用，皆與天子同；指使承順，如奉天子同。人間福分享受，無不窮極；獨恨不能淫樂女色，所少者此耳。嘗命左右，訪有復生陽物之方，購以萬金。
paragraphs.en: The court time and again heeds ministers who preach profit and sends eunuchs out across the country to levy duties on goods—in the name of “taxing merchants and curbing the secondary trades to strengthen agriculture, the root.” In truth, when taxes on trade are heavy, goods grow dear wherever they are resold: prices rise for the buyer, and the buyer suffers. When trade stops moving, goods grow cheap where they are produced: prices fall for the seller, and the seller suffers. The profit may seem to come only from merchants, but all four classes of the people are silently bled of their wealth to feed the court’s hidden exactions—worse than openly raising the land tax. Worse still, of every levy taken, the court gets one share, the eunuch ten, the tax officials a hundred, and the patrol guards a thousand. So the people pay out hundreds or thousands of taels to deliver a single tael to the court: little gained above, measureless harm below. And yet, when runners and tax clerks stuff their bottomless gullets, at least it is folk of this same realm who get fed and warmed. But men who neither plow nor weave and yet make fish and meat of the common people are nothing but grubs, battening on the food and clothing of the world. As for the eunuchs: having plundered and squeezed until their hoards pile high and overflow, they look on brocade as dead leaves and on gold and jade as rubble. Their dress, their food, their vessels all match the Son of Heaven’s, and the minions at their beck and call wait on them as they would wait on the Son of Heaven. Of every blessing and pleasure the human world holds, they enjoy the uttermost; their one regret is that they cannot have the pleasure of women—that alone is denied them. One of them once bade his attendants hunt for a method to regrow the male organ, with ten thousand taels as the reward.

paragraphs.zh: 有方外道士，利得其金也，私臆懸度，謂「古方云『土以土補，木以木補，人以人補』，意必食人可補人也。」妄去獻方云：「烹童男膾肝脯肉，食其精髓，則精液充滿，陽物復生，可姦婦生子矣。」閩高閹信之，先售以百金，候服有驗，再來領萬金。由是，命牙爪往窮鄉僻邑，買貧民幼童，詐云「高衙欲養為子，日後富貴無窮。」貧民信之，多賣以博眼前重利，且希望後日富貴。後先買者，難以稽數。但鬻子之家，有託人往​​查己子者，並無聲息；即衙中走僕，亦不知內之養子若何也。原來買之幼童，盡養以錦衣美食。廚子能烹調一童以進食，賞銀十兩，深禁其秘密。每殺一童，廚子提刀追趕，眾童各涕泣奔呼，候其走熱氣揚，則執其肥者烹之。
paragraphs.en: A wandering Daoist, greedy for that gold, made a wild guess of his own: “The old formulas say earth is mended with earth, wood is mended with wood, man is mended with man—so eating human flesh must mend a man.” He went recklessly and offered up a recipe: “Boil a young boy, mince the liver, dry the flesh, and eat the essence and marrow. Then the vital fluid will be replenished, the organ will grow back, and you can lie with women and father sons.” The eunuch Gao of Fujian believed him. He paid a hundred taels up front; if the dose proved effective, the man could return for ten thousand taels. From then on he sent his henchmen into poor villages and remote counties to buy young boys from destitute families, lying that “the Gao household wants to raise them as sons, and later they will have wealth and honor without end.” The poor believed it, and many sold their sons for the heavy profit in hand, hoping besides for riches to come. How many were bought in all is impossible to reckon. But some of the families who had sold sons sent people to ask after their boys—and there was never any word. Even the servants who ran errands in the yamen had no idea how the adopted sons inside were faring. In fact, the purchased boys were all kept in brocade and fed the finest food. Any cook who could prepare a boy for the table was rewarded with ten taels, and the secret was guarded under the strictest ban. Each time a boy was to be killed, the cook chased the children with a knife while they ran weeping and screaming; when they had run themselves hot and their blood was up, he seized a fat one and cooked him.

paragraphs.zh: 內有一童十二歲，跪廚子涕泣哀告，叩頭求救。廚子亦淚曰：「吾怎能救你，吾亦不奈何墮此也。」有頃，外人傳某鄉官相拜。廚子曰：「憑你命，吾放你出去，外有鄉官相拜，你扯其衣死哀求救；肯帶你去，則你可生，我代你死罷。你可傳知外人，切勿將子賣入太監府也。」此幼童直奔至鄉官前，哀告：「廚子要殺我！」太監即令查拿廚子斬首，———彼恨其縱出此童也，笑顏諭幼童入後。幼童死扯鄉官衣求救。鄉官疑有緣故，為之帶出。幼童歷敘內中殺諸童之由，鄉官不勝嗟嘆。思起本未得諸童買來之由，又無廚子證據，亦不敢留養此童，遣其出外別投生。此童後流丐於建郡等處。人問其太監府之事，多能言其中之富貴，皆非人世所有也。自後方知太監之食人，始不肯以子賣之。近年，高閹以罪去。其鬻子之父母，累十百候於途，並不見一幼子與姦閹生去者，無不墮淚，痛其子之必遭烹也。
paragraphs.en: Among the boys was one of twelve who knelt before the cook, weeping and pleading, knocking his head on the ground and begging for his life. The cook wept too: “How could I save you? I fell into this against my own will as well.” Presently word came from outside that a certain retired official had come to pay a call. The cook said: “I will leave it to your fate: I am letting you out. A retired official is calling—grab his sleeve and wail for your life. If he will take you away, you may live, and I will die in your place. And tell the people outside: never sell a son into a eunuch’s house.” The boy ran straight to the official and cried out, “The cook is going to kill me!” The eunuch at once ordered the cook seized and beheaded—he hated him for letting the boy slip out—and with a smiling face commanded the boy to return inside. The boy clung desperately to the official’s sleeve, begging to be saved. The official suspected there was more behind it and took the boy out with him. The boy recounted in full how the children inside were being slaughtered, and the official sighed without end. But reflecting that he had never learned how the boys had been bought in the first place, and that with the cook dead there was no witness, he dared not keep the boy himself; he sent him out to find some other way to live. The boy later drifted as a beggar around Jian Prefecture and thereabouts. When people asked him about the eunuch’s household, he could tell them much of the wealth and splendor within—things this world has never seen. Only then did people learn that the eunuch ate human flesh, and only then did they refuse to sell their sons. In recent years Eunuch Gao was removed for his crimes. The parents who had sold their sons waited along the road in scores and hundreds, and not one saw a young son come out alive with that vile eunuch. There was none who did not shed tears, grieving that his boy must surely have been cooked.

paragraphs.zh: 按：貧民賣子，極為至愚。若不能養，何不若鳳陽府父子俱丐，猶可骨肉相保。必不得已，唯可賣之富戶為僕。固不可供太監之啖，亦不可賣入庵寺為行童侍者，其賤尤在乞丐下也。國家置閹尹，以供掃除傳命耳。至使握利權，享用已極，更思生陽物淫婦人，為不可必得之事。雖食人而可為汝欲扶已朽之軀，曾不惜人渾全之命乎？是可忍也，孰不可忍也！孟子曰：「善戰者服上刑」，猶為強兵而殺人也；此為何事而視人命如草菅乎？王法若明，當不令此閹得生還矣。
paragraphs.en: Note: For poor people to sell their sons is folly of the deepest kind. If you cannot raise them, why not do as they do in Fengyang Prefecture, where father and son beg together? At least flesh and blood stay together. If there is truly no other way, sell them only to a rich household as servants. You must never feed them to a eunuch’s appetite, nor sell them into convents and temples as boy servants and attendants—that degradation is lower than beggary itself. The state keeps eunuchs to sweep the palace and carry messages, nothing more. To let them grasp the power of profit, glut themselves on every luxury, and then attempt to restore their virility so they can debauch women—a thing they cannot possibly have! Even if eating human flesh could feed your lust and prop up your rotting carcass, have you no pity for another person’s whole and unbroken life? If this can be endured, what cannot be endured? Mencius said, “Those skilled in war should suffer the heaviest punishment”—and that was for killing to make an army strong. What cause is this, that human lives should be treated as weeds? If the law of the land were truly enforced, this eunuch would never have been allowed to return alive.

stories.title_en: Faking an In-Person Silver Handover to the Education Commissioner

paragraphs.zh: 凡学道出巡，各处棍徒云集追随，专体探富家子有谋钻刺者，多方献门路，以图蛊骗。或此路不售，后一帮又生一端以投，年年有堕其术者。但受骗之家羞以告人，故后次人又蹈之。
paragraphs.en: Whenever the Provincial Education Commissioner goes on tour, crooks from every quarter gather and follow him, hunting for rich men’s sons who want to buy influence. They offer openings of every kind, hoping to cheat them. If one pitch does not take, another gang comes along with a different angle; every year some fall for it. But the families who are cheated are too ashamed to tell anyone, so the next people walk into the same trap.

paragraphs.zh: 有一学道，考选至公，不纳分上。忽一棍自言能通于道者，人不之信。棍曰：“此道爷自开私门，最不喜人央分上前途。唯对手干者，百发百中，但人不敢耳。如真肯干者，但要现钱，彼当面接之，可稳保成就。”赵甲问曰：“从何处献之？”棍曰：“候退堂后，先用手本开具某县某人银若干，求取进学。彼肯面允，便进上银；如不允，银在我手，彼奈我何？”赵甲曰：“我要在旁亲看。”棍曰：“自然与你亲看。学道的二门，其缝阔一寸，从外窥之，直见堂上，任你看之。”赵甲曰：“若道肯亲手接银，吾敢投之。”即写手本，以手帕包银二百两作一封。
paragraphs.en: There was an education commissioner, scrupulously fair in his examinations, who took no private requests. Suddenly a con man claimed he could channel directly to the commissioner; no one believed him. The con man said, “This commissioner has opened a private door himself. He hates it when people send introductions through intermediaries. Only those who deal with him face-to-face succeed every time—people just don’t dare. If you truly mean to do it, all you need is ready money; he’ll take it in person, and success is as good as guaranteed.” Zhao Jia asked, “Where do we present it?” The con man said, “Wait until he leaves the hall. First use a petition listing such-and-such county, so-and-so, so many taels of silver, asking to be admitted to the school. If he agrees in person, then hand over the silver; if he doesn’t, the silver remains in my hands—what can he do to me?” Zhao Jia said, “I want to stand beside you and watch for myself.” The con man said, “Of course you’ll watch for yourself. The second gate of the education commissioner’s office has a crack an inch wide; peeking from outside you can see straight into the hall—watch as you wish.” Zhao Jia said, “If the commissioner will take the silver with his own hands, I’ll dare to go in.” He wrote a petition and wrapped two hundred taels in a handkerchief as one packet.

paragraphs.zh: 下午出堂，往道前候之。棍曰：“要二包过门银。”甲付与之。将退堂之际，棍以银与手本挨入堂去，嘱甲曰：“才封门时，即要在门缝来看。”及道退堂后，甲于二门缝中看，见道仍旧纱帽圆领而出。棍先以手本高递上，一门子接进。道展看了，笼入袖中去。棍又高擎一封银上，道顾门子，门子接上银。道一看即转身，门子随后捧银包而入。棍趋至二门，隔门谓甲曰：“好了，好了，事已妥矣！你见否？”甲应曰：“我亲见了，果是自接。”棍曰：“今夜不能出，我你须在门内外宿矣。”甲曰：“但得事妥，不吃晚饭亦好。”
paragraphs.en: That afternoon they went out and waited in front of the commissioner's office. The con man said, "I need two packets of silver to get through the gate." Jia paid him. As the session was about to end, the con man took the silver and the petition and slipped into the hall, telling Jia, "The moment they seal the gate, come look through the crack." After the commissioner left the hall, Jia looked through the crack in the second gate and saw a man still in gauze cap and round-collared robe come out. The con man first held the petition high; a yamen attendant took it in. The commissioner opened it, looked it over, and tucked it into his sleeve. The con man then held a packet of silver high; the commissioner glanced at the attendant; the attendant took up the silver. The commissioner glanced at it and turned; the attendant followed him in, carrying the silver packet. The con man hurried to the second gate and said through the door, "It's done, it's done! Did you see?" Jia said, "I saw it myself; he did take it with his own hands." The con man said, "I can't go out tonight; you and I will have to sleep on either side of the gate." Jia said, "If the business is settled, going without supper is fine."

paragraphs.zh: 次日开早门，棍与甲方同出，即到甲店拜贺。甲大设席待之。棍曰：“高取后须厚谢我。”甲曰：“加一谢是定规，不加亦不减矣。”此为信棍之戒。
paragraphs.en: The next morning, when the early gate opened, the con man and Jia went out together and visited Jia’s shop to celebrate his success. Jia hosted a lavish feast. The con man said, "Once you secure your winnings, you must reward me generously." Jia replied, "Adding an extra thank-you gift is the fixed rule; I won’t add anything beyond that, nor will I subtract anything." Let this serve as a warning against trusting crooks.

paragraphs.zh: 后揭晓日，本生无名。棍查不见踪，方知前受银之道，乃此棍先与宿衙人套定，盖妆假道也。
paragraphs.en: On the day the results were announced, the victim's name was nowhere to be found. The swindler had vanished. Only then did they realize that the way the silver had been taken earlier was because this swindler had first colluded with the night-duty yamen men to stage a fake official.

paragraphs.zh: 二门望入堂上，虽可亲见，终是路遥，哪见得真？故落此棍骗而不知。若真道自接银，何必衣冠出？何必堂上递手本？又何必堂上交银？独不可私递手本乎？况堂上有宿衙人役，岂私受银之地？此村富不识官体，故以目见为稳，不知与你目见，正所以骗你也。
paragraphs.en: Looking from the second gate into the hall, though you can see it yourself, the distance is still great—how can you see clearly? So they fell for this swindle without realizing it. If an official were truly accepting silver personally, why come out in full dress? Why present a petition in the hall? Why hand over silver in the hall? Couldn't the petition be passed privately? Besides, the hall has staff on duty—is that a place to accept silver in secret? This rustic rich man did not understand official protocol, so he took seeing with his own eyes as proof; he did not realize that letting you see with your own eyes was exactly how they cheated you.

stories.title_en: The Swindler's Seal: A Trick in a Retired Official's Private Quarters

paragraphs.zh: 富人钱一，欲为子买进学。歇家孙丙，有意骗之，与之言曰：“此中李乡官，原与学道同僚，二人极相得。今若说一名进学，此断可得。吾试与商议之。”钱一曰：“可。”孙丙往匠铺，见两挂箱一样，用钱三钱买其一，又以银二分定后只，嘱曰：“我停会引人来买，更出三钱，不可别换。”又买两把一样的锁。后以挂箱与锁付李乡官家人曰：“你可秤定二百两石头，装在挂箱内，外加锁之，放在你家主房内。少顷，我领人央你老爷说进学，以二百两好银与你封。你把放银的箱收入，换放石的箱出来，然后将这银与我均分。”李家人许曰：“可。”
paragraphs.en: Rich man Qian Yi wanted to buy his son a place in the school. Innkeeper Sun Bing intended to cheat him and said, "There is a retired official named Li here who was once a colleague of the education commissioner; the two are very close. If we speak up for one candidate, we can certainly secure admission. Let me try discussing it with him." Qian Yi said, "All right." Sun Bing went to a craftsman's shop, saw two identical chests, bought one for three qian, and paid a deposit of two fen to reserve the second, telling them, "In a moment I'll bring someone to buy it; he will pay another three qian—do not swap it for a different one." He also bought two identical locks. Then he gave a chest and lock to Official Li's servant: "Weigh out two hundred taels of stones, put them in the chest, lock it from the outside, and place it in your master's room. Shortly I will bring someone asking your master to speak for school admission, bringing two hundred taels of good silver for you to seal. You take in the chest with the silver, swap it for the chest with the stones, then split this silver with me." Li's servant agreed: "All right."

paragraphs.zh: 孙丙领李家人来，对钱一说：“我面见李老爷了，他道此事容易，只把现银对于他家人看过锁住，送到他家加封条，仍以银箱付还我，以锁匙付他收。待有名进学之后，将原银谢他，不得开箱再换。”钱一曰：“在你家借一挂箱来用。”孙丙曰：“新锁有，挂箱可往街买之。”领钱一家人，以银三钱，往铺买到。钱一将银二百两同李家人、孙丙三面对定，收入挂箱中，外加锁定。
paragraphs.en: Sun Bing brought Li’s servant and told Qian Yi: “I met Lord Li in person. He said this is easy: have the ready silver shown to his servant, checked and locked, sent to his house to be sealed, then return the silver chest to me while giving him the key to keep. Once he passes the examination and enters the academy, the original silver will serve as his thanks; the chest must not be opened or swapped.” Qian Yi said, “I’ll borrow a chest from your place.” Sun Bing replied, “I have a new lock; you can buy the chest at a shop.” He led one of Qian’s men, paid three qian, and bought it. With Li’s servant and Sun Bing watching, Qian Yi verified two hundred taels of silver, placed them in the chest, and locked it securely.

paragraphs.zh: 孙丙负银，同钱一到李乡官家，求加封条。李乡官推病，在厅左房内坐。李家人持箱入门边曰：“银已看对阴白，只讨一封条。”李乡官曰：“既看明白，还他自收，来接封条。”李家人仍以银箱出，再领出一封条，对三面封讫。钱一解锁匙，付李家人收。孙丙复负银箱归，交与钱一自收藏，皆谓事极妥矣。
paragraphs.en: Sun Bing carried the silver chest with Qian Yi to Official Li’s house, requesting a sealing strip. Official Li feigned illness and sat in a room to the left of the hall. Li’s servant held the chest at the doorway: "The silver has been verified against the mark; we only need one sealing strip." Official Li replied, "Since it’s been checked clearly, give it back for him to keep, and come fetch the sealing strip." The servant took the chest out again, then brought out a sealing strip and sealed all three sides before them. Qian Yi handed over the key to Li’s servant. Sun Bing carried the silver chest back and gave it to Qian Yi to store away; everyone thought the matter perfectly secure.

paragraphs.zh: 及揭晓，钱一子无名。孙丙曰：“事不成，银现在，可速收拾归，免得李家人来索轿价。”钱一既失望，怏怏而归。及到半路，叫匠人开锁启视，则皆石头矣。惊异复回，大闹歇家曰：“你何通同骗我？”孙丙曰：“我与你当面干事，何处是骗你？若三面共开挂箱，犹怪得李家；今去半日，私自开箱，我那知中间是银是石？”钱一明知是孙、李合骗，只事无凭证，谅是难取，但辱骂歇家一场而归。此为信乡官之戒。
paragraphs.en: When the results were posted, Qian Yi's son had no name on the list. Sun Bing said, "It didn't work; the silver is still here. Pack up and head home quickly, lest Li's people come asking for sedan-chair fees." Qian Yi, disappointed, headed home dejected. Halfway there he called a carpenter to open the lock and look: all stones. Shocked, he went back and made a scene at the inn: "How did you collude to cheat me?" Sun Bing said, "I did the business with you face to face; where was the cheat? If the three of us had opened the chest together, you could still blame the Li household; now after half a day's travel you opened the chest in private—how would I know whether inside was silver or stone?" Qian Yi knew perfectly well that Sun and Li had cheated him together, but there was no proof; he figured the silver would be hard to recover, so he only cursed the innkeeper roundly and headed home. Take this as a lesson: do not trust retired officials.

paragraphs.zh: 按：两挂箱共样，本是难辨。但加封条，只须在外封之，何必持入内禀乃请封条乎？向令当时若告，追究卖挂箱之家，问两箱何以一样，或能证出孙丙先买其一，后领人买一。或遇明官，便可从中勘出换包之骗矣。
paragraphs.en: Note: Two chests of identical pattern are naturally hard to distinguish. Yet applying a seal only requires doing so on the outside; why carry them inside to report and then request the seal? Had the victim reported it to the magistrate at the time, investigating the shop that sold the chests and asking why two were alike might have revealed that Sun Bing first bought one, then arranged for another to be purchased. With a clear-sighted official, the package-swap swindle could have been exposed from this.

paragraphs.zh: 建宁府郝天广，世家巨富，有几所庄，多系白米。时建宁无价，其智家罗五闻省城米价高腾，邀主人带二仆，以米十馀船装往省粜。时宗主王爷发牌考延、建二府，各有告示，将考儒童。米才上船，有一客人带二仆，来搭船往省。船中暇坐，问其何干。答曰：“王爷家来投书者。”后又谈及可夤缘之事，天广有长子出考，言甚合意；只宗主前考甚公，并无私窦，未敢深信其事。
paragraphs.en: Hao Tianguang of Jianning Prefecture came from an old wealthy family with several estates, mostly stocked with white rice. At the time, rice prices in Jianning were low; his steward Luo Wu heard that prices in the provincial capital were soaring and invited his master, along with two servants, to load ten-odd boats of rice to sell there. Just then, Chief Examiner Lord Wang had issued orders to examine students from both Yanping and Jianning prefectures, with proclamations announcing the civil service exams for young scholars. As the rice was just being loaded, a guest accompanied by two servants arrived to book passage to the capital. Seated at leisure on the boat, they asked what his business was. He replied, "I have come from Lord Wang's household to deliver a letter." Later, the conversation turned to securing favors through connections. Tianguang had his eldest son taking the exam; the talk suited him well. However, since Chief Examiner Wang had conducted the previous examinations very fairly, with no backdoor channels, he did not quite dare to believe it.

paragraphs.zh: 至省中，棍辞别去，曰：“王爷有公子在学，必共看卷。试与谈尊府事，倘许诺，我再出回你诺；若不出，则事不谐耳，再亦无信。”天广曰：“是也。”密遣一仆，踪迹棍所去处，果入学道衙去。数日后出来曰：“事谐矣。可将银对定，以我皮箱藏之，外加封条，银仍与你自收掌。后有名进学，即以皮箱银交出与我。”天广思“银虽对定，仍是我藏，有何不可？”即依言对讫，不知此棍有甚法。银明是天广自投自锁，棍只加封票一条而去，再约曰：“今夜间公子或可潜出，我与之同看过，事即美矣。”连候数夜不来，天广以皮箱开看，其内尽是砖石，前银已被赚去矣。此为封银防换之戒。
paragraphs.en: At the provincial capital, the crook took his leave: "Lord Wang has a son in the school; they are sure to look at papers together. I'll try talking about your honorable house; if he agrees, I'll come out and bring you the yes; if I don't come out, the matter isn't on, and there will be no further word." Tianguang said, "Right." He secretly sent a servant to track where the crook went; indeed he went into the Education Commissioner's yamen. After several days he came out: "It's arranged. Weigh out the silver, hide it in my leather case, add a sealing strip outside; the silver stays in your own keeping. After the name is on the list for school, you hand the leather case of silver over to me." Tianguang thought, "Though the silver is checked, I still keep it—what's wrong with that?" He followed the instructions and weighed it out, not knowing what method this crook had. The silver was clearly put in and locked by Tianguang himself; the crook only added one sealing ticket and left, and further agreed: "Tonight the young master may slip out; I'll look it over with him, and the matter will be fine." They waited several nights; he did not come. Tianguang opened the leather case: all bricks and stones; the silver had been cheated away. Let this be a warning: when sealing silver, guard against a swap.

paragraphs.zh: 按：买进学、买帮补，甚至买举人，此事处处有之，岁岁有之，而建宁一府，叠遭骗害为甚。盖建郡民富财多，性浮轻轻故也。虽累受骗，而继起营买者未已，此光棍途中常以逢考建宁为一桩好生意也。特其封银法，至今人看不破。明以银与之同封，复还我收，及棍去后开之，则皆砖石矣；或以为有一遁银法。如此神矣哉，上智难防也！唯明鉴乎此，勿信为上。若急欲买进，可勿封银，须以榜上有名为定。若只信其漏报，虽至三四次见金榜矣，亦未可以银付之，方可防其脱也。
paragraphs.en: Note: Buying a school place, buying a stipend, even buying the juren degree—this happens everywhere, every year, and Jianning Prefecture has been cheated over and over, worse than anywhere else. The people of Jian commandery are rich with much wealth, and their nature is light and flighty. Though they have been cheated again and again, those who follow up to buy still do not stop; so sharps on the road often treat the Jianning exams as a lucrative business. The method of sealing silver, especially, people still cannot see through to this day. Clearly, you seal the silver together, it is given back for you to keep, and after the crook leaves, you open it—all bricks and stones. Some think there is a method of making silver vanish. How miraculous—even the wisest can hardly guard against it! Only see this clearly; not believing is best. If you urgently want to buy entry, don't seal silver; take a name on the posted list as the settlement. If you only believe his leaked reports, even if you see the golden list three or four times, you still must not hand over silver; only then can you guard against being cheated out of it.

stories.title_en: Sealing Silver in an Empty House, Then a Staged Robbery

paragraphs.zh: 骗局多端，唯仕进一途，竟奔者多，故遭骗者众。棍尝有言，唯虚名可骗实利，唯虚声可赚实物。盖仕进之人，求名之心胜，虽掷重利不暇顾惜，遂入棍术中而不及察。
paragraphs.en: Swindles take many forms; yet in the path of official advancement, so many rush headlong that the number of victims is vast. Swindlers often say: only an empty name can cheat one out of solid profit; only hollow reputation can earn real goods. For those seeking office, their hunger for fame is so intense that they throw down heavy sums without pausing to consider, thus falling into the swindler's trap without noticing.

paragraphs.zh: 有一巨富家子，欲营谋进学，所带管家者极为能干。往省考大续，寓一歇家中，令其求关通之路。数日内，以门路投者，更进迭来。管家者窥其行径，穷其来历，皆察其言事不相应，踪迹不分明，多与歇家有套同情弊，悉拒却之，不信其哄。后一棍妆为仆价，言语迟钝，举动村朴，自方跟一罢职乡官，与宗主有旧，来此打秋风。引管家去见乡官，果似贫薄小官样。面酌定一名进学，只谢银一百两亦肯讲，只要现银，来伊店封。管家曰：“在我店封。”乡官曰：“事宜慎密，你店内人众，传扬不便。此下有一所空房，是顾秀才的，前欲在彼借寓，以借什物不便，故迁在此。可与我小价在彼处封定，最是稳当。”管家强求乡官来所住店看封为妥。乡官曰：“汝更有疑，我只小价一人，任你多用人来同封。”管家回以“外人不可与知，只同本主去。”果只村仆一人在，把银出对定。忽有棍数人，打开门入曰：“汝辈买秀才，吾拿去出首！”将三人打倒，银尽抢去。
paragraphs.en: A wealthy family's son sought to scheme his way into the academy; the steward he brought was extremely capable. They traveled to the provincial capital for the examination and lodged at an inn, instructing the steward to find a way through. Within days, various people offering connections arrived one after another. The steward observed their conduct, traced their backgrounds, and found their words inconsistent with their actions, their tracks unclear, and many colluding with the innkeeper. He rejected them all, refusing to believe their lies. Later, a crook dressed as a servant, slow of speech and rustic in manner, claimed he followed a dismissed country official who had old ties with the Chief Examiner and had come here to seek financial aid. He led the steward to see the official, who indeed looked like a poor minor official. They agreed face-to-face on one name for the academy; even a hundred taels as a bribe he would discuss, provided it was ready silver, sealed at his inn. The steward said, "Seal it at my inn." The official replied, "The matter must be discreet; your inn has too many people, making it inconvenient if word spreads. Down below there is an empty house belonging to Xiucai Gu. I intended to lodge there before, but borrowing furnishings was inconvenient, so I moved here. You and my little servant can seal the deal there; that is most secure." The steward insisted the official come to their inn to witness the sealing. The official said, "If you still doubt, I have only one little servant; you may send as many people as you like to seal together." The steward replied, "Outsiders must not know; I will only go with my master." Indeed, only the rustic servant was present. They brought out the silver and checked it. Suddenly several crooks burst in: "You are buying a xiucai! We'll take you and report it!" They beat the three men down and robbed all the silver.

paragraphs.zh: 村仆爬起，做烦恼样。管家起，挈其手曰：“不须恼，此银亦不多，同在我店再封。”村仆不肯去。富子曰：“事已错矣，何可再干？”管家曰：“我自有处。”强邀村仆再来，一面令富子速收拾回家。管家雇募店中人，将自己当作儒士，与村仆对锁，送入县中，口告被脱抢之故。县官曰：“你不合买进学，与者受者各有其罪。况被棍抢银，与乡官家人何干？”管家曰：“抢银者即此棍之伙。但穷究此银出，情愿追入官；更愿大罚，与此棍同罪。”县官再差人去叫乡官，早已走了。县官曰：“此果是棍。”严刑拷打。棍仆受刑不过，愿赔一半。追完，管家又告愿全追，甘与同配驿。棍仆死不肯摊出同伙；又累受刑，无可追。乃将棍仆拟徒，管家者只拟杖发归。此为封银防抢之戒。
paragraphs.en: The rustic servant got up, putting on a distressed look. The steward rose, took his hand, and said, “Don’t worry; this silver isn’t much. Come to my inn with me, and we’ll seal it again.” The servant refused to go. The rich son said, “The matter has already gone wrong; how can we do it again?” The steward replied, “I have a way.” He forced the servant to return, while simultaneously telling the rich son to pack up and head home quickly. The steward hired men from the inn, passed himself off as a scholar, had them lock themselves together with the rustic servant, and sent them to the county yamen, where he verbally accused them of being robbed. The magistrate said, “You shouldn’t have bought into the scholar-official class; both giver and receiver are guilty. Besides, being robbed by crooks—what does that have to do with a retired official’s servant?” The steward said, “The robbers were this crook’s accomplices. Only thoroughly investigate where this silver came from; I am willing to have it recovered for the government, and I am also willing to be heavily fined, sharing the same crime as this crook.” The magistrate then sent people to summon the retired official, but he had already fled. The magistrate declared, “This is indeed a crook,” and ordered harsh torture. The servant-crook could not bear the punishment and agreed to repay half. After recovering that amount, the steward again petitioned, demanding full recovery and willing to accept joint exile to a garrison station. The servant-crook would rather die than name his accomplices; tortured repeatedly, nothing more could be recovered. Thus, the servant-crook was sentenced to penal servitude, while the steward received only beating and was released. This serves as a warning: when sealing silver, guard against robbery.

paragraphs.zh: 按：管家虽有能，终落棍所脱抢。特既抢后，即能拿棍仆同解，甘与同罪，终能追其一半，棍亦无所利。若富子自己，必不肯与棍同罪，而一抢之后，无如之何矣。或曰：管家顶认儒士，若官考之何如？曰：央分上之人，已是天才，官何须考？即考不得，亦无妨也。
paragraphs.en: Note: Although the steward was capable, he ultimately fell victim to the swindler's theft. However, after the robbery, if he were willing to arrest the swindler and accept joint liability for the crime, he could eventually recover half the money, leaving the swindler with no profit. If it had been the rich son himself, he would surely refuse to share the blame with the swindler; once robbed, there would be nothing to be done. Some ask: What if the steward claimed to be a scholar? How would the official test him? Answer: A man who secures influence through connections is already a master of the game; why would the official need to test him? Even if he failed the exam, it wouldn't matter.

stories.title_en: Impersonating a Favor-Seeking Guest to Solicit Exam Bribes

paragraphs.zh: 简学宪最廉明。考大续时，有秋风客到，寓于开明僧舍。次日，有一棍带三仆来，亦与同寓。内中相拜，自称彼系县堂亲眷，亦来打秋风者。外则炫耀冠服，仆从扔卫更盛，每与（冠）盖往来寺中。尝有生儒遇之，辄误指曰：“此学道乡亲也。”又见简道亲回拜，又请酒，偕真秋风客往，而棍专外影窃其名，以欺诳人。简公是严明人，不数日，真秋风客已打发行矣，唯棍在寺。其外棍伙故四下传扬曰：“学爷乡亲在某寺。”生儒中亦甚传之，多有求取大续者，只无人可担当银。棍背套学道衙中书手、皂隶来，过付银封于其家。人既信是真秋风客，又衙门有身役人与同事，银封其家，亦复何虑？棍客动云，彼要说十名，每名要三百两。当赴场人众，各务兢趋，数日已满十人之数。共日封于各书、皂之家，明白交付，共银三千两。背地各瓜分已讫。
paragraphs.en: Education Commissioner Jian was renowned for his integrity and clear judgment. During the student renewal examinations, a favor-seeking visitor arrived and lodged in the monks' quarters at Kaiming Temple. The next day, a swindler arrived with three servants and took lodgings there as well. Inside the temple they exchanged courtesy calls, and the swindler claimed to be a relative of the county magistrate who had also come to solicit favors. Outwardly, he flaunted splendid robes and caps, with a retinue even grander than the other's, frequently coming and going through the temple under official canopies. Students who saw him often mistook him, saying, "This is the Education Commissioner's hometown relative." When they saw Commissioner Jian's real relative return a courtesy call and invite him for wine, the swindler tagged along with the genuine visitor while secretly borrowing his name on the outside to deceive people. Commissioner Jian was a strict and upright official, and within a few days the genuine favor-seeker was sent on his way, leaving only the swindler at the temple. His outside accomplices deliberately spread word everywhere: "The Education Commissioner's hometown relative is staying at such-and-such temple." The rumor circulated widely among the candidates; many who wished to buy a place in the examination were eager to pay, yet lacked a reliable person to handle the silver. Behind the scenes, the swindler colluded with clerks and runners from the Education Commissioner's yamen, having them come forward so the silver could be sealed and deposited at their homes. Since people already believed he was the genuine relative, and since official yamen staff were involved, what was there to worry about in sealing the silver at their houses? The swindler announced that he could secure ten places at three hundred taels each. With so many candidates competing eagerly, the quota of ten was filled within days. On the appointed day, the silver—three thousand taels in all—was openly checked, sealed, and deposited at the various clerks' and runners' homes; behind the scenes, the gang divided the spoils at once.

paragraphs.zh: 但思后日无名，不能回复诸人，银亦何以得去？乃雇一人，往学道出首：“见得衙门书、皂某某等，外同客棍招揽生童银若干两，封于某某等家。”简准状，即出白牌，提拿客棍风火至急，秋风棍即乘机逃去。又拿在衙书皂拶夹，皆不肯招，各打三十，革役。又差人往衙役家搜缉。凡有名与列钻刺者，闻踪迹露出，唯恐指名逮捕，各各四散，走回本县，银都弃撇，不敢来问。由是棍得安享所分之银。书皂虽革役，无赃可据，后复陆续谋入。唯一时受夹打，彼刑用在衙人役，亦仅如搬戏；而所得之多，奚止偿失也！此为信秋风客之戒。
paragraphs.en: But they thought: later, if they have no name to give, they cannot answer anyone—and how will they get the silver away? So they hired someone to go to the Education Office and report: "Clerks and runners so-and-so of the yamen, together with an outside traveling swindler, solicited so many taels from students, sealed at so-and-so’s homes." Jian accepted the complaint, issued a plain warrant to seize the traveling swindler with utmost haste; the Autumn Wind Swindler then used the chance to flee. Then they seized the yamen clerks and runners, put them to the squeezers and presses; none would confess; each was beaten thirty strokes and dismissed. They sent men to search the yamen staff’s homes. Anyone named as having bought their position, hearing their tracks were exposed, feared being named and arrested, scattered in all directions, fled back to their home counties, abandoned the silver, and dared not come ask. Thus the swindler could enjoy in peace the silver he’d split. The clerks and runners, though dismissed, had no stolen goods that could be proven; later they gradually schemed their way back in. They only suffered squeezing and beating for a time; using punishment on yamen staff is also just like putting on a play; and what they got was more than enough to repay the loss! Let this serve as a warning against trusting the Autumn Wind Swindler.

paragraphs.zh: 按：此棍称学道乡亲，而学道既已来拜，又请吃酒，则的是乡亲矣。况书、皂皆有身役人，为之翼护，人孰疑之？不知真乡亲已去，而此乃其托名者。彼衙门人唯利是图，所敛既多，何惜数十之板？况其顶头银仍在，虽革役，乌足以惩之。今人谓衙役知法，不知侮法者正是知法之人。唯蹈实地行实事，以真学问博真功名，勿萌侥幸，勿图钻刺，棍骗何从入哉？彼遭骗者，皆惰学不肖之徒，自取灾眚者也。
paragraphs.en: Note: This crook claimed to be the education commissioner’s hometown relative. Since the commissioner had already visited and invited him to drink, he truly seemed a hometown relative. Besides, clerks and runners all held official posts, shielding him—who would suspect? They didn’t know the real relative had departed, and this was merely someone borrowing his name. Those yamen men care only for profit; having collected so much, what did they care about enduring a few dozen strokes of the cane? Moreover, the silver they paid to buy their posts remains intact; even if dismissed, how could that serve as punishment? People today say yamen runners know the law; they fail to realize that those who abuse the law are precisely those who know it best. Only walk on solid ground, do solid things, and win true fame through true learning. Do not sprout hopes of lucky breaks, nor plot to buy influence—how then could swindles take hold? Those who are cheated are all lazy, unworthy students who bring disaster upon themselves.

stories.title_en: Silver Left with an Innkeeper, Who Steals It and Flees

paragraphs.zh: 有三棍合帮，共骗得银三百两，未肯遂分，更留合装骗棚，以图大骗。先遣一人过省，离会城两日之府，用银七十两买屋，内系土库，城外铺舍开一客店。又用银五十两娶一妻，买一婢，又买一家奴。更有数十两在手上，调度供家。人见其店有家着奴婢，食用丰足，多往宿其店。此府相近省城，往年文宗考科举不及，常调邻府生童到此合考，以便往返，每富家生童择店，必居于此。
paragraphs.en: Three crooks in a gang cheated out of three hundred taels together but refused to split them; instead, they pooled the silver to set up a front for a bigger swindle. First, they sent one man across the province to a prefecture two days from the capital, where he spent seventy taels to buy a house with an earthen storehouse inside and opened shop premises outside the wall as a guest inn. Another fifty taels went toward marrying a wife, buying a maid, and purchasing a male slave. They kept several tens of taels on hand for household expenses. Seeing that the inn had a family, servants, and abundant provisions, many travelers chose to stay there. This prefecture was near the provincial capital; in previous years, when the provincial examinations were held elsewhere, students from neighboring prefectures were often transferred here for joint exams to make travel easier. Consequently, wealthy students selecting an inn invariably stayed at this one.

paragraphs.zh: 壬子科六月，科期已迫，复调外两府生员来此选考。本店住建郡三个秀才，皆系巨富。一日，有客儒人品丰厚，衣冠鲜整，泊船城外，入此店来，密问店主曰：“你识科举秀才中有大家者乎？”店主曰：“我店中三位都富家，你问何干？”客儒曰：“有好事与他讲。”店主曰：“甚好事，何不对我说？”客儒曰：“你不在行，只好与秀才讲。”店主出，向三秀才曰：“此客先生问科举秀才何人最富，有好事对他说。我问他何事，又不肯言。列位试问其说何事。”三人共入叙礼，问曰：“老丈问富家，小弟等家皆万金，有何好事说？”客曰：“列位肯计较中否？”三秀才曰：“中都肯计较，兄有何门路？”客曰：“我亦不能为力，亦不识门路。但果肯计较者，各备银一千两，来此店对过封定，付还你收，自有指示的路。”三人约四日后家中取银来对，客儒辞去。三人密遣人跟随客去，见其下船，船中止一家人。归报如此，三秀才喜曰：“此必大主考的人，可信也。”店主出问：“适间说何事？”三秀才曰：“此未必然事，若事可成，自有大抬举你。”
paragraphs.en: In the sixth month of a Renzi year, with the exam deadline pressing, students from two outer prefectures were again summoned here for selection. Three xiucai from Jian commandery resided at our inn, all men of great wealth. One day, a visiting scholar, impressive in appearance and neatly dressed, moored his boat outside the city wall and entered the inn. He asked the innkeeper in secret: "Do you know among the exam xiucai any from wealthy families?" The innkeeper replied: "The three in my inn are all rich; why do you ask?" The guest said: "I have a good matter to discuss with them." The innkeeper asked: "What good matter? Why not tell me?" The guest replied: "You are not versed in this matter; I can only speak with the xiucai." The innkeeper went out and told the three: "This gentleman asked which of the exam xiucai is the richest; he has a good matter to share. When I asked what it was, he refused to say. You gentlemen should try asking him." The three went in, exchanged courtesies, and asked: "You asked about rich families; our households each possess ten thousand taels; what good matter is there?" The guest said: "Would you gentlemen be willing to negotiate the arrangement?" The three replied: "We are all willing to negotiate; what channel do you have, brother?" The guest said: "I cannot act on my own, nor do I know a channel. But if you truly wish to negotiate, each prepare one thousand taels, come to this inn, verify the silver and seal it, then hand it back for you to keep; a path will be pointed out." The three agreed to fetch the silver from home in four days to verify; the visiting scholar departed. The three secretly sent someone to follow him; they saw him board a boat where only one servant remained. They reported this; the three rejoiced: "This must be an associate of the chief examiner; he can be trusted." The innkeeper came out and asked: "What did you just discuss?" The three replied: "This is not yet certain; if the matter succeeds, we will ensure you are greatly elevated."

paragraphs.zh: 四日后，三家人都取银到。客儒应期来问，各答“银都齐备。”客曰：“今夜对明封定。”三秀才言：“银多夜间不便，明日入店主内庭去对。”客曰：“店主恐不密事，不知外客房中封更密。”三秀才曰：“明日临时相商。”客辞去。夜饭后，店主出曰：“列位与此客议封银事，客人难防。这门壁浅薄，若夜间统人来劫，可要提防。依我说，可藏入我城门内，你外间好心关防，可保安稳。”三秀才曰：“是也。”共将六皮箱银都寄入店主家内去。家主瞒过妻婢，将银尽从后门藏出，与棍伙夤夜逃去。唯嘱其妻曰：“明日三秀才问我，只说早间出去寻人，少刻即归。”
paragraphs.en: Four days later, the servants from all three households arrived with the silver. The visiting scholar came on schedule to inquire, and each of the three scholars replied, "The silver is all ready." The visitor said, "Tonight let us verify it under bright light and seal it." The three scholars said, "There is a great deal of silver, which makes nighttime inconvenient; tomorrow let us go into the innkeeper's inner courtyard to verify it." The visitor said, "The innkeeper may not keep this matter confidential; sealing it in the outer guest rooms would be more discreet." The three scholars said, "Let us discuss it when the time comes tomorrow." The visitor took his leave. After supper, the innkeeper came out and said, "You gentlemen were discussing sealing silver with that visitor—traveling strangers are hard to guard against. These doors and walls are thin; if they bring a gang to rob you in the night, you must be on your guard. In my opinion, you should store the silver inside my house within the city gate while you keep watch outside; that will be completely secure." The three scholars agreed and entrusted all six leather chests of silver to the innkeeper's house. Concealing it from his wife and maid, the innkeeper slipped all the silver out through the back door and fled late at night with the gang of crooks. Before leaving, he merely instructed his wife: "Tomorrow, if the three scholars ask for me, just tell them I went out early to look for someone and will be back shortly."

paragraphs.zh: 次日，客儒欣欣喜色来对银。秀才曰：“银付店主收藏，今早出外，少待即归。”等到午间，店主不回。客辞归船。午后又遣家人来问，又以店主未归答之。至第三日午间，问店主妇取皮箱，妇答云：“并未见甚箱。”及出溪边寻客船，亦不见矣。再问店妇取，苦执未见。任入搜之，竟不见踪。问：“店主果何去？”妇云：“前夜已出，教我如此应你。”三人正慌。
paragraphs.en: The next day, the visiting scholar arrived in high spirits to weigh and verify the silver. The scholars said, "We gave the silver to the innkeeper for safekeeping; he went out early this morning and will be back shortly." They waited until noon, but the innkeeper did not return, so the visitor went back to his boat. In the afternoon, the visitor sent his servant to ask again, and once more they answered that the innkeeper had not yet returned. At noon on the third day, the scholars asked the innkeeper's wife for the leather chests, but she replied, "I have never seen any chests." When they went out to the riverbank to look for the visitor's boat, it too had vanished. They questioned the innkeeper's wife again, and she stubbornly insisted she knew nothing of the chests. She let them search the house as they pleased, yet not a trace was found. "Where did the innkeeper really go?" they demanded. The wife replied, "He left the night before last and told me to answer you this way." The three scholars were thrown into a panic.

paragraphs.zh: 适此三棍脱得银去，已出境外。晚投宿一店，店主见其来晚，提其六箱皆重，疑是窃贼，明日将集众擒之。三棍闻其动静，次早天未明，只挑得四箱去，以二箱寄店。店主越疑是贼，出首于官。太府将银逐封开之，内封有一合同文书，称某人买举人者。太府提某生员到，不敢认。太府以甘言赚之，乃招认，即收入监。后又投分上解释，再骗去银四百两方免申道。又没入店主之屋，及官卖其妻婢，并箱内一千都追入库。彼四箱被棍挑去者，幸得落名，不受再骗。是府官亦一棍也。此为信店家一戒。
paragraphs.en: By then these three crooks, having made off with the silver, were already out of the territory. At night they lodged at an inn. The innkeeper saw they came late, hefted the six cases—all heavy—and suspected they were thieves; he planned to gather people to seize them the next day. The three heard the stir; next morning before dawn they carried off only four cases and left two at the inn. The innkeeper became even more convinced they were thieves and reported them to the officials. The prefect opened the silver packets one by one; inside one seal was a contract document stating that so-and-so was buying a juren degree. The prefect summoned that student; he dared not admit it. The prefect lured him with sweet words until he confessed, whereupon he was thrown into jail. Later, he sought connections to settle the matter but was cheated out of another four hundred taels before they would refrain from reporting it to the commissioner. They also confiscated the innkeeper’s house, sold his wife and maid by official order, and recovered the thousand taels in the cases into the treasury. The four cases the crooks carried off luckily had no names on them, so those students were not cheated again. Thus the prefectural official was also a crook. Let this serve as a warning to innkeepers.

paragraphs.zh: 按：店主有家眷，最可凭者。彼肯代藏银，孰不信之？谁知其妻妾皆买下以装棍棚者。彼骗得厚利，则弃此而去，别娶妻妾，享大富贵矣。以有眷属之店尚不可信，世路之险，一至于此！人若何不务实而可信棍以行险哉！
paragraphs.en: Note: An innkeeper with a family is the most reliable. If he agrees to store your silver, who wouldn't trust him? Yet who would guess that his wives and concubines were all purchased merely to play the part of the crook's accomplices? Once he has reaped a fat profit, he abandons them and departs, marrying new wives and concubines to enjoy great wealth. Even an innkeeper with dependents cannot be trusted—the perils of the road have reached such extremes! Why do people not stick to honest work, instead trusting crooks to gamble on dangerous paths?
